10141-a-discourse-on-the-life-character-:
William Cullen Bryant, the poet and editor, gave this memorial address before the New-York Historical Society on May 17, 1870. Its subject was Gulian Crommelin Verplanck, a New York lawyer, scholar, and public man who had just died after a long useful life. The Society asked Bryant to print the address at once.

Bryant traces Verplanck's work in law, letters, and civic life, praising steady service over show. He presents a man whose learning and manners helped shape New York's public mind. Readers get a graceful, period portrait of a respected citizen, and of the city he served.
10517-government-and-rebellion-a-sermon-:
Rev. E. E. Adams preached this sermon in the North Broad Street Presbyterian Church on Sunday morning, April 28, 1861, just after the Civil War began. Published by request, it takes Proverbs 17:11 as text: an evil man seeks only rebellion, and a cruel messenger shall be sent against him. Adams treats rebellion as a crime against God and government.

Adams argues that God never pardons a rebel until he repents and submits, and that people need not pronounce forgiveness until an enemy shows sorrow and stops wrongdoing. A child's rebellion against a parent offers his homely parallel. Readers get a firm, wartime sermon on law, repentance, and Union.
10698-the-aeroplane-boys-on-the-wing-or-:
John Luther Langworthy sent Frank and Andy Bird to the tropics in The Aeroplane Boys on the Wing, published in 1912. The Bird boys, already known to readers of the series, chase a clue that leads to a strange "devil-bird," an airship launch, an air chase, and a camp in the tropical jungle. Guards, firebrands, and jaguars add danger on the ground.

Langworthy writes fast, plain adventure for boys, with the aeroplane itself as the hero's tool. The book is an early example of aviation fiction, written when flying was barely a decade old. Young readers get thrills, teamwork, and exotic places, all from the cockpit of a new machine.
11153-no-hero:
E. W. Hornung wrote this 1903 novel, whose narrator insists his story is unheroic, told in the modern manner from the latest possible point. The book opens with a waiter bringing the narrator a fatal letter from Catherine Evers, the first for years from a once constant correspondent. The narrator, a young man about town on two walking-sticks in 1900, studies the unopened envelope, whose handwriting gives no hint of its news.

Chapters follow a plenipotentiary, the theatre of war, first blood, a marked woman, second fiddle, prayers and parables, the lion's mouth, a stern chase, and number three. Bob Evers tells the narrator that his talk of being mere pals with a woman was rot, as he shaves with razor in mid-air. Hornung, creator of Raffles, writes a wry tale of love, honour, and self-knowledge.
11256-social-life-at-rome-in-the-age-of-:
W. Warde Fowler's study of social life at Rome in Cicero's age fills a gap he saw in English scholarship. readers knew Roman politics, but not Roman manners, education, morals, and religion in the last age of the Republic. Drawing on Cicero's nine hundred surviving letters, the richest social archive from classical antiquity, Fowler reconstructs daily life, households, friendships, and public conduct. Marquardt's Privatleben der Römer supports his account.

Fowler planned the book as a companion to a life of ancient Athens, then finished it as a standalone educational work. Its argument is that Cicero's age matters as much as the Empire's, as a critical moment in Graeco-Roman civilization. Classicists still cite it as an accessible introduction to late Republican society.
11448-cicero:
W. Lucas Collins's Cicero, in the Ancient Classics for English Readers series, surveys the Roman orator's life and work in twelve chapters, from early life and education through the impeachment of Verres. the consulship and Catiline, exile and return, relations with Caesar and Antony, character as politician and orator, correspondence, essays on old age and friendship, philosophy, and religion. Collins acknowledges Forsyth's Life of Cicero and Long's scholarly volumes, taking responsibility for translations.

Collins opens by noting ancient means different things for Homer's infant society and for Cicero's late Republic. His volume aims at general readers, not scholars, summarizing a large career compactly. Students meeting Cicero for the first time will find it a clear, Victorian introduction.
12140-roman-farm-management-the-treatise:
Published in 1918, this volume gives English versions of two Roman farm manuals. Cato wrote on agriculture in the second century BCE, and Varro wrote three books on rural affairs a century later. A Virginia farmer made the translations, with notes that link old practice to his own day. Both books address owners who ran farms with hired hands and enslaved labor.

Cato moves from buying land and laying out a farm to the duties of overseer and housekeeper, soil care, crops, vines, olives, livestock, and even curing hams. Varro divides his subject into the farm itself, its equipment and workers, and its animals, with long passages on fences, water, buildings, and breeding. Together they show how Romans judged soil, planned labor, and weighed profit against pleasure in country life.
13481-roman-life-in-the-days-of-cicero:
The Rev. Alfred J. Church writes Roman life in the days of Cicero as scenes, not as a formal biography or a history of the late Republic. Chapters follow a Roman boy, an undergraduate, a magistrate, a great cause, country life, a great conspiracy, Caesar, Pompey, exile, and Cato, Brutus, and Porcia.

Verres the governor, feasting in Syracuse, seizes a captured pirate prize for himself and deals with young and old by practical greed. Caesar swims to a ship with a manuscript held clear of the water and his cloak in his teeth, then orders a tribe massacred without hesitation. Church lets such scenes show Roman law, war, and politics through the eyes of Cicero's age.
13509-grappling-with-the-monster-or-the-:
T. S. Arthur, author of Ten Nights in a Bar-Room, grapples with strong drink in this temperance volume, subtitled the curse and the cure. He admits embarrassment at the mass of material, with every chapter fit to grow into a book of its own. Illustrations trace the steps from youth to manhood, a confirmed drunkard, and old age as a total wreck.

Arthur shows how moderate drinkers slip into excess, as a depraved appetite strives for mastery from the first indulgence and no man who indulges is absolutely safe. Dr. R. P. Harris adds a chapter on tobacco as an incitant to alcohol and an obstacle to reform. The book is a full Victorian case against drink, built from stories, warnings, and cures.
14260-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Volume six of The Great Events by Famous Historians gathers episodes from the Middle Ages. It opens with a note on its binding, a copy of a work by Geoffroy Tory for King Francis the First. Tory, a teacher of letters, set up a press in 1518 and printed Greek and Latin books. The volume moves from episode to episode, told by a historian. It aims to let readers meet the past through scenes.

One episode tells how bishops preached the Fourth Crusade against the Greeks as foes of Rome. Clergy urged war as just, drove women from camp, and set men to confession before the assault. Another episode treats the Mise of Lewes, which freed war prisoners and held princes Edward and Henry as hostages. About five thousand men are said to have fallen on each side at Lewes. The book gives war, law, and faith in strokes.
14682-my-friend-prospero:
Henry Harland's 1904 romance My Friend Prospero opens with a coach drawing up before an Italian castle gateway, where Lady Blanchemain considers a formal garden in April weather. John Lane published the novel in London and New York.

Prospero, a miller in the Austrian sense, a bourgeois without coat-armour, courts Annunziata amid terraced gardens, mimosa, and blackcaps, while society warns against a match across rank. Harland writes with light irony about class and love. The novel is a charming comedy of manners, set in an Italy of gardens and old houses.
14903-the-knights-of-the-white-shield-up:
Edward A. Rand's 1886 boys' book, first in the Up-the-Ladder Club series and dedicated to Ken and the other boys, tells how a club is made. A grand march, an offer for Sunday school scholars, a pammerrammer and the nation's birthday follow, with a sick patriot and a nailed door and window.

An entertainment, a cupola, Aunt Stanshy's boarder and a club in splinters lead to a club mended, a knight going to sea, a trap, a fair and a fire. Rand, author of school and camp series, writes club life as moral adventure: boys learning loyalty, leadership and fair play. The white shield stands for a standard the knights try, and sometimes fail, to live up to.
15122-the-little-colonel-s-hero:
Annie Fellows Johnston's 1902 children's novel brings back Lloyd, the Little Colonel of a Kentucky valley home, for her twelfth birthday. The day opens in gloom: her mother lies ill, her father has gone to town, and no one seems to recall the date. Only her pony Tarbaby offers comfort as she rides down a locust-lined avenue.

What looks like neglect soon turns into surprise, and Lloyd learns lessons in patience, pluck, and kindness through the year that follows. Johnston writes in a warm Southern voice, with dialect speech and country detail. Young readers meet a heroine who grows by facing hurt feelings and small trials with grace.
15202-young-folks-treasury-volume-2-of-1:
Edited by Hamilton Wright Mabie, with Edward Everett Hale as associate editor, this second volume of Young Folks' Treasury gathers myths and legendary heroes for children. Advisers include university presidents, a cardinal, and former presidents Roosevelt and Cleveland. An illustration shows Jason hurling his helmet.

Greek heroes, Norse tales, and other world myths appear in retellings suited to young readers, with heroism, cunning, and wonder at the fore. The series aimed to give children a noble stock of stories. Parents and teachers still use the volume as a solid, old-fashioned introduction to myth.
15359-the-negro:
W. E. B. Du Bois published this history in New York in 1915, with maps of Africa and its peoples. It opens by calling Africa at once the most romantic and the most tragic of continents, then traces its ancient kingdoms, its peoples, and its long contact with Europe and Asia. The book was written for general readers, not only for scholars.

Later parts follow the slave trade, the growth of Black life in America, and the struggle for freedom and full citizenship. Du Bois blends geography, history, and argument, pressing the case that Black history begins in Africa, not in slavery. As an early short history by a leading Black scholar, it still reads as both an introduction and a claim: that this past deserves study on its own terms.
15946-the-original-fables-of-la-fontaine:
La Fontaine's original fables, rendered into English prose by Frederick Colin Tilney, with coloured pictures by the author. J. M. Dent and Sons issued the book in London, with E. P. Dutton in New York, as part of Tales for Children from Many Lands, edited by F. C. Tilney. The fables come in plain prose, not verse, for young readers. Pictures by Tilney himself join the text.

The Two Mules, The Hare and the Partridge, and The Gardener and his Landlord open the set. The Man and his Image, The Animals Sick of the Plague, and The Unhappily Married Man follow, with The Rat Retired from the World, The Maiden, and The Wishes. The Dairy-Woman and her Pail of Milk and The Priest and the Corpse close the sample. The book gives La Fontaine's wit in easy English: beasts that teach men.
1642-euthyphro:
Plato's Euthyphro, translated by Benjamin Jowett, opens in the porch of the King Archon, where Socrates awaits his trial for impiety and meets Euthyphro, a diviner prosecuting his own father for murder. Socrates asks Euthyphro what piety itself is, and the diviner's answers unravel under questioning.

Is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because loved? The question, still called the Euthyphro dilemma, drives the dialogue to an open end. The work is a brief, perfect introduction to Socratic method, and to philosophy's first questions about gods and goodness.
16440-the-water-supply-of-the-el-paso-an:
J. L. Campbell's engineering paper tackles a dry-country problem: how to water a railway across 128 miles of New Mexico desert between Carrizozo and Santa Rosa. Rain there averaged under ten inches a year, and well water on the line was poor. The road crossed no streams for hundreds of miles in either direction from El Paso.

Campbell sets out the new supply scheme, with wells, quality tests, and figures, followed by discussion from fellow engineers. The paper is technical and full of tables, aimed at civil engineers rather than casual readers. It stands as a clear record of how railways solved water supply in the arid Southwest.
16605-the-ladies-work-book-containing-in:
John Cassell of London put out this how-to book for home needlework, with steps for knitting, crochet, and point lace. It shows how to cast on, purl, join pieces, form rounds, and cast off, then gives plans for mats, covers, tidies, curtains, and small dress items. Drawings walk the reader through each stitch.

The book is a workbench guide, not a tale: each plan states the stitch, the shape, and the finish in plain order. It suits a reader who wants to make useful house goods by hand, from a baby shoe to a bed quilt. Its value today lies in its clear old craft methods and its full range of home projects.
16626-letters-to-helen-impressions-of-an:
Keith Henderson, an artist on the Western Front, writes to Helen from France in this 1917 volume, with his own illustrations. A first letter, June 6, 1916, finds him on the slowest train that ever limped, after seven hours' sleep, with twenty-eight hours still to go. Crucifix Corner, Bailleul, Fricourt Cemetery, trenches, a wounded tank, and Peronne fill the pictures.

Henderson writes as a painter-soldier, noting color, ruin, and odd beauty amid war. His letters are short and vivid, with secrecy about ports and places. The book gives the Great War through an artist's eyes, tender and unsparing at once.
16672-the-last-journals-of-david-livings:
Horace Waller edited David Livingstone's last journals in Central Africa, volume one covering 1866 to 1868. The journals were saved after the explorer's death, with a narrative of his last moments by his servants Chuma and Susi. Chapter one arrives at Zanzibar, meets the sultan, and faces the slave market, tsetse fly, and sepoys' trouble on the road inland.

Waller's introduction recalls the hope that some journals might survive the disaster. The journals give Africa in Livingstone's own daily words: lakes, peoples, and hardships. Readers of exploration will find a moving, first-hand record of the great traveler's final years.
17024-the-last-journals-of-david-livings:
Horace Waller edited this second volume of David Livingstone's last journals, covering 1869 to his death in 1873. It opens with illness, a slow trip to Ujiji, and a puzzling current in Lake Tanganyika, then follows new probes toward the Lualaba and the Manyuema country. Susi and Chuma, his faithful servants, add a closing tale of his last days and sufferings.

The journals mix fever, desertion, Arab traders, and elephant hunts with notes on peoples, rivers, and beasts. Livingstone writes in short, tired entries that still carry wonder. For readers of exploration, this is the raw, moving end of a great African career, told in the explorer's own worn words.
17042-illustration-of-the-method-of-reco:
This Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology paper, under director J. W. Powell, shows the method of recording Indian languages, drawn from manuscripts of J. O. Dorsey, A. S. Gatschet, and S. R. Riggs. It opens with an Omaha myth, How the Rabbit Caught the Sun in a Trap, obtained from F. LaFleche by Dorsey, printed in a phonetic script with marks for raised, turned, and dotted letters.

The paper teaches field workers how to write Native speech sounds with exact signs, so words can be read true after the speaker is gone. Its symbols, explained in a transcriber's note, cover nasals, stops, and vowels. Linguists and historians of Native America will find a key early methods paper, short, technical, and full of worked examples.
17370-prehistoric-textile-fabrics-of-the:
William H. Holmes's Bureau of Ethnology paper studies prehistoric textile fabrics of the United States as seen in impressions on pottery. Groups run from cord-marked vessels in Pennsylvania and New York to fabrics from Arizona, Kentucky caves, Swiss lake dwellings, and Ohio mounds. Figures show coffee sacking threads, sections, and ancient cloth patterns pressed into clay.

Holmes reads each impression for weave, thread, and method, turning potsherds into textile history. His paper suits archaeologists and craft lovers who want to see lost cloth through clay. Short and richly pictured, it remains a classic early study of how ancient Americans wove, long before any cloth survived.
18113-history-of-the-expedition-to-russi:
General Count Philippe de Ségur wrote this History of the Expedition to Russia, undertaken by Napoleon in 1812, in a second revised edition printed in London in 1825. Ségur dedicates the work to the veterans of the Grand Army, comrades disarmed by the northern ice.

Book one traces the politics of France and Russia since 1807, with Prussia, Turkey, and Sweden in view. Later books follow the march, the battles, and the dread retreat from Moscow. Ségur writes as a soldier who was there, with grief and pride. It is a classic, first-hand history of the 1812 disaster, still read for its vivid, tragic force.
18279-the-composition-of-indian-geograph:
J. Hammond Trumbull published this 1870 study of place names drawn from the Algonkin languages of North America. Trumbull opens by rejecting the idea that a proper name is a mere mark with no meaning. In the native languages of America, he says, every name of a person or a place must keep the sense of its roots.

A name, on his account, must state its meaning with precision to all who speak the language. When sound change or changed circumstance strips a name of that self-defining power, the language drops it. The essay therefore reads place names as small pieces of grammar and history, and shows readers how to hear the meaning still held in them.
18472-the-amours-of-zeokinizul-king-of-t:
This little work presents itself as a translation from the Arabic of the famous traveller Krinelbol, with a key, printed in London for G. Smith near Temple Bar in 1749 at one shilling and sixpence. The preface insists that the translator has mixed nothing of his own into the amours of Zeokinizul, king of the Kofirans.

The book is a satirical romance of a king's loves, told as if from an eastern source, with a key inviting readers to match its characters to figures nearer home. Its charm lies in that game of disguise, where an exotic tale carries a sharp look at court life, love, and power in the author's own world.
1863-notes-on-a-journey-from-cornhill-to:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Notes on a Journey from Cornhill to Grand Cairo records his 1844 voyage from London to Egypt, by way of Vigo, Lisbon, Cadiz, Gibraltar, Athens, Smyrna, and Constantinople. The Lady Mary Wood carries him through the Mediterranean, and his chapters mix travel notes with satire on fellow passengers.

Thackeray watches card players quarrelling three hours before noon, armed to the teeth and afraid to fight. He notes that they are bred from the same land that begot philosophers and heroes. The book is travel writing with a novelist's eye, funny about hotels, guides, and ruins, and fond of the East even while it laughs at the tourist.
19800-london-and-the-kingdom-volume-1-a-:
Reginald R. Sharpe, the City of London's archivist, wrote London and the Kingdom. Volume one builds the history mainly from the City's own archives. Sharpe surveys what earlier writers covered: trade and craft guilds, for instance. He lists the powers of the Courts of Aldermen and Common Council. Church history, he notes, others handled well. His own ground is the City's records.

London's archives are among the richest any city keeps. Sharpe spent his career ordering and calendaring them. A history drawn from records corrects legend with paper. Guilds, courts, and the livery companies fill these pages. The book serves anyone tracing London's self-government. It is institutional history written by its keeper.
20990-london-and-the-kingdom-volume-2-a-:
Buckingham's murder, a forced loan, and four aldermen jailed crowd volume two's contents. Reginald Sharpe's London and the Kingdom draws its tale mainly from the City's own archives. The Long Parliament, Strafford, and Scottish envoys fill its Civil War years.

Sharpe, the City's records clerk, knew London's papers as few men did. Charters, letters, and council acts give his history its firm spine. Volume two runs from Charles the First to the Commonwealth's storms. Readers get London as a power in the land, proud, rich, and courted by kings and parliaments alike.
21206-the-romany-rye-a-sequel-to-lavengr:
George Borrow continues Lavengro in The Romany Rye, issued here in the 1900 Ward, Lock edition with an introduction by Theodore Watts-Dunton. Borrow opens with an advertisement answering critics who claimed Lavengro was cooked up against the popish agitation of 1850-51. He says the main part was written in 1843.

The sequel follows Borrow's wandering hero among gypsies, horse fairs, and roadside folk, mixing real travel with fiction. Romany language and lore run through it, as in Borrow's books on Spain. Its famous appendix defends his earlier work and attacks his critics. The title names a gypsy gentleman, which the hero in some sense becomes.
21380-a-young-hero:
Phil Carleton, eight or nine, sits over his Latin with grey, anxious Dr Martin. The French scholar in a black silk cap teaches him in George Manville Fenn's short tale. War between England and France is about to break over Canada, where they live. Phil's father, an English officer, suddenly arrives with hard orders.

The doctor must abandon his house, books, and papers at once and take the boy through hostile country to the English lines. Days of privation and insult from farmers follow, then arrest as supposed spies. In the end a battle comes, and the dying General Wolfe is brought drafts of water by young Phil himself.
22877-lavengro:
Scholar, Gypsy, and Priest walk through Lavengro, George Borrow's strange and famous book. Borrow warns readers on his title page not to merge the three figures into one. Something of the Gypsy may show in the Scholar, he grants. Nothing of the Priest shows in either, he insists.

Part novel, part memoir, the book follows a young word-lover through England and Wales. He learns Romany, boxes, tinkers, argues theology, and collects people the way others collect coins. Language itself is the real hero, with Gypsy speech honored throughout. Lavengro baffled and charmed its first readers in 1851. It still does both, and its road scenes remain among the most alive in English prose.
22878-lavengro:
Borrow's Lavengro continues in this second hosted portion of his roaming, bookish life. A voice in the excerpt muses on wishes and misery. The fulfilment of one's wishes, he has heard, is invariably the forerunner of extreme misery. A life without hope or wish, he adds, would be more horrible still.

That mix of road talk and reflection marks the whole work. Borrow drifts among Gypsies, priests, tinkers, and scholars, trading stories and arguments at every stop. Philology and fist fights sit comfortably side by side. Readers joining the book here should know it rewards wandering rather than plot. Taken slowly, the pages give a vanished England of lanes, fairs, and campfires, recorded by a man who loved its margins.
2812-letters-of-marcus-tullius-cicero:
This volume collects the surviving letters of Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman of the late Republic. Written to friends, family, and political allies, the letters cover elections, trials, exile, civil war, and the daily business of Roman life. They show Cicero arguing, worrying, and joking in his own voice rather than in the polished manner of his published speeches.

Readers gain a close view of Rome's last republican decades, including games with elephants that left crowds pitying the animals. The letters also reveal friendships and rivalries that shaped public decisions. The collection remains a central source for Roman history and a model of the familiar letter as a historical document.
3114-the-education-of-the-negro:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote The Education of the Negro as an address on Black citizenship and schooling after emancipation. Warner notes that about five million Black people entered citizenship at the war's close, growing to over seven and a half million by the 1890 census. He uses the word negro as descriptive, distinguishing African peoples from other black or colored races such as Abyssinians.

Warner credits the race with humor, good humor, and capacity for devotion, testified by southerners during the Civil War, and argues those distinct traits might contribute to a cosmopolitan civilization. The address reflects its era's racial language and paternalism, while urging education as the path forward. It remains a document of post-Reconstruction debate over Black schooling.
4516-peter-a-novel-of-which-he-is-not-th:
F. Hopkinson Smith tells this novel through a friend who watches Peter, a bank clerk poring over his ledger late one December afternoon. Peter, bald and grey-browed, has kept the same walk uptown with the narrator for years, and the sight of him still at his desk after four o'clock signals trouble. The title warns readers at once that Peter, for all his presence, is not quite the hero of his own tale.

Through bank work, friendships, and quiet acts of character, Smith builds a warm portrait of an ordinary man caught in larger events. The narrator's fond, observant voice gives the book its charm, as small daily habits reveal loyalty, worry, and decency. Readers get a gentle American novel about friendship and work, where the most interesting man in the room is not always the one who drives the plot.
5816-successful-exploration-through-the-:
Successful Exploration Through the Interior of Australia recounts a great overland journey, opening with a biographical sketch of birth, infancy, boyhood, education, and youthful traits. A second chapter sends two sons from England to Australia, with voyage incidents, journal extracts, arrival at Port Phillip, and Melbourne life. Shepherd work in the interior, Melbourne in 1853, and advice to immigrants follow.

Readers follow explorers from home to outback, through stations, deserts, and the slow work of mapping a continent. The book blends biography, journal, and practical guidance, giving a full picture of colonial Australia in the 1850s. It suits readers of exploration history and Australian history, offering a detailed, firsthand-flavored account of a famous interior crossing.
6391-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Two celebrated families, Calvini and Aenobarbi, spring from the race of the Domitii, and Nero belongs to the second, Suetonius begins. The Aenobarbi take name and descent from Lucius Domitius. Met on his road to Rome by two young men of august appearance, he was bidden to announce a victory not yet known in the city. To prove themselves more than mortal, they stroked his cheeks and turned his black hair bright as brass, a mark passed to his posterity.

Nero Claudius Caesar's life, in Thomson's translation revised by Forester, runs from that omen to an emperor's reign of informers, treason charges, and Greek crowns demanded as equivalents. Lawyers who drew wills for a prince's profit faced fines, and purple colours were forbidden to others while agents bought in secret. Suetonius writes Nero as a prince whose art and cruelty both became law.
8857-the-life-studies-and-works-of-benja:
John Galt composes this 1820 life of Benjamin West, president of the Royal Academy of London, from materials furnished by West himself, and inscribes it to Alexander Gordon. Galt's preface explains that West's professional life formed part of a larger historical work. It could only appear as an episode, and that he once meant to prepare the whole memoirs separately. A careful review of the manuscript, he says, changed his plan into this volume.

Part one follows West from his Pennsylvania Quaker boyhood, through his early painting in America, to London, royal patronage, and the presidency of the Academy. Galt, novelist and friend, writes with firsthand warmth about an artist who painted American history for a British king. The life remains a key source on West and on the art world of Georgian London, best read beside West's paintings themselves.
9847-bacon-is-shake-speare-together-with:
Sir Edwin Durning-Lawrence wrote Bacon Is Shake-Speare in 1910, arguing that Francis Bacon wrote the plays known as Shakespeare's. The book opens by calling the plays the greatest birth of time and their author the greatest genius of all ages. Classical scholars, Durning-Lawrence notes, marvel at the plays' lore, while lawyers rank their author among law's great minds. From such learning, he builds his case for Bacon.

The volume also reprints Bacon's Promus of Formularies and Elegancies, collated from the original manuscript. Plates from Sylva Sylvarum add visual evidence. A reader gets a classic statement of the Baconian heresy, and a window on how fiercely authorship debates once burned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-capec:
Alfonso Capecelatro was a cardinal, Archbishop of Capua, and writer, born at Marseilles in February 1824 and dead in November 1912. He descended from the dukes of Castel Pagano. His father, a Napoleonic officer under Murat, fled to Malta and Marseilles when Ferdinand of Naples repressed political liberalism. The family went back to Italy in 1826 and Naples in 1830. Capecelatro gave himself to ecclesiastical studies, especially ecclesiastical history, and to charitable enterprises.

He was drawn to St. Peter Damian, St. Catherine of Siena, St. Philip Neri, and St. Alphonsus Liguori, figures of Italian revival, whose biographies he wrote. He answered Renan's Life of Christ and published his own Life of Jesus Christ, gathering modern research on Hebrew topography and customs, without polemics. He also wrote three volumes on Catholic doctrine, two on the Christian virtues, and sermons. Leo XIII made him assistant librarian at Rome, Archbishop of Capua in 1880, and cardinal in 1885.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alghero:
Alghero is an Italian diocese of twenty-two communes in Sassari province and four in that of Cagliari, in the Archdiocese of Sassari. Genoa's Doria family built the city in 1102, and in 1106 John, Bishop of Alghero, attended the Trinity Church consecration at Sacargia. After a long period of decadence Julius II renewed and confirmed the see by his Bull of 1503.

The Genoese Pietro Parens took the bishopric and sat at the Lateran Council of 1512 from its first through its seventh session. The diocese holds 20 parishes, 71 secular priests, and 54,300 inhabitants today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonsus-de-:
Alphonsus de Castro, Friar Minor, born at Zamora in 1495, died at Brussels in 1558. At fifteen he entered a Franciscan convent near Salamanca. He taught theology at Salamanca, serving forty-three years as confessor to Charles V and Philip II and preacher at Spain's court. In 1545 he accompanied Cardinal Grennis to Trent, prominent in the fourth session on Scripture.

As the cardinal's representative he subscribed to its canons. He proposed adding to the Decree on Canonical Scriptures that besides sacred books much else must be held, unwritten, by Church authority. In later sessions he addressed vernacular Scripture and original sin. He accompanied Philip II to England, returning with him in 1557. Appointed to Compostella after Cardinal John Tolenton's death, he died before taking office. Best-known works: Against All Heresies (Cologne 1539) and On the Just Punishment of Heretics (Salamanca 1547). Both appeared in one Paris edition (1571-78).
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-apari:
Antonio Aparisi, a Spanish lawyer and speaker born in Valencia in 1815 and dead in Madrid in 1872, stands at the centre of this Catholic Encyclopedia life story. Trained for the bar in 1839, he won most of his criminal cases and wrote poems and pieces for Catholic papers in Valencia and Madrid. As a deputy for Valencia in the Cortes, the Spanish parliament, he led the royalist group. He spoke for Catholic unity and the pope's temporal power, meaning the pope's rule over land in Italy.

Later work took him to Paris and London on dynastic business, and to a Carlist meeting in Switzerland in 1870. He also wrote treatises with titles such as El Papa y Napoleón and La cuestión dinástica, and he was elected a senator from Guipuzcoa in 1871. His collected works came out in five volumes after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barbastro:
Barbastro is a suffragan diocese in Spain, its city standing where the Cinca and Vero rivers meet. Roman Hither Spain once held it, and Arabs under Muza took it in 711, giving the name Barbaschter, source of Barbastrum. Saracens held it until about 1063, when Sancho Ramirez of Aragon retook it. After further Arab seizures, Pedro I restored it to Spain in 1101 and, with papal consent, moved the see there from Roda.

Its first bishop, Poncio, went to Rome to secure permission for the transfer. The diocese, bounded by the Pyrenees, Lérida, Huesca, and Yaca, holds 154 parishes under ten archpriests. About 240,000 people live there, served by some 220 clergy in 231 churches and 177 chapels. King Ramiro the Monk abdicated there in 1134, and its cathedral, palace, seminary, and Piarist college rank among its noted buildings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolome-de-:
Bartolomé de Torres Naharro was a Spanish poet and dramatist born at Torres, near Badajoz, toward the end of the fifteenth century. A cleric of some learning, he lived at Rome about 1514 as chaplain to his patron Fabricio Colonna. A satire attacking the Court's vices got him banished from Rome, and he took refuge at Naples. There in 1517 appeared his Propaladia, collecting lyrics, satires, epistles, romances, ballads, and eight plays he called Comedias.

Beyond literary merit, the plays matter for his dramatic theory, a model later authors followed. He split comedies into Noticia, from real seen happenings, and Fantasía, from imaginary incidents seeming true. He kept Horace's five acts, renamed Jornadas as mere resting places, and required six to twelve characters. Some plays tend toward the unities of time, place, and action, and his best-known comedies are Himenea, Serafina, and Tinelaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benito-jeroni:
Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro, a celebrated Spanish Benedictine writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Galicia in 1676, he died at Oviedo in 1764 after taking the Benedictine habit at San Juan de Samos in 1688. His learning ranged across nearly every branch of knowledge of his day.

Feijóo attacked old customs, superstitions, and stale institutions, and pressed for reform of public teaching in Spain. His essays made him a voice of the Spanish Enlightenment, though he wrote as a monk. The entry presents a critic who used wide reading to clear away error, and who paid for candour with controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bertinoro:
Bertinoro, a small city in Romagna, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Anciently Forum Truentinorum, and Petra Honorii in the Gothic war, it takes its present name from that second title. Legend says St. Illuminata of Ravenna fled there about 303 but still met martyrdom.

Until 1360 Bertinoro obeyed the Bishop of Forlimpopoli, but when Cardinal Albornoz destroyed that city, the bishop's seat moved to Bertinoro. The entry first sketches Forlimpopoli, founded in 173 BC, then follows Bertinoro's bishops and churches. It is a compact diocesan history built on a transfer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-borgo-san-sep:
Borgo San-Sepolcro, a diocese in Arezzo province, Tuscany, grew around a tenth-century oratory built by two pilgrims home from Palestine. They set relics from the holy places there, pilgrims flocked in, and a town rose around the shrine, later ruled in time by the abbot of a Camaldoli monastery. Guido Petramala, Bishop of Arezzo, walled it and made it a Ghibelline stronghold.

Subject first to Castello, it became a see under Leo X in 1515, with Giovanni Galeotto Graziani as first bishop. Later bishops include the theologians Nicolo Tornabuoni and Dionisio Bussotti and Gian Lorenzo Tilli, founder of the seminary. Its cathedral, a three-nave Romanesque church leaning toward Gothic, holds the famed Volto Santo, a great wooden crucifix in a long tunic, kept there since the tenth century. The diocese counts 60,500 Catholics and 250 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catanzaro:
Catanzaro is the capital of Calabria and the seat of a diocese suffragan to Reggio. The date its see was erected is uncertain, but it may go back to 1122, when Pope Callistus II moved the see of Taverna to Catanzaro. The diocese then counted 85,000 people, with 48 parishes and 97 churches and chapels.

Its clergy numbered 116 secular and 4 regular priests, and it held one religious house of men and five of women. The whole entry is a compact statistical portrait of the diocese, giving its size, its parishes, and its clergy without a longer historical narrative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cattaro:
Cattaro is the chief town of one of Dalmatia's four divisions. It is set beneath steep limestone cliffs on a small Adriatic bay, nearly ringed by mountains. Its gulf, the Bocche di Cattaro, counts among Europe's most picturesque sites. The ancients called the town Ascrivium, and it became a Roman colony early in the Christian era before Saracens destroyed it around 860.

Refugees driven from home by the Hungarians rebuilt it. Cattaro was a republic by the twelfth century. It passed under Byzantine and Serbian rule, allied with King Louis of Hungary in 1368, and submitted to Venice in 1423 while keeping some autonomy. The diocese, suffragan to Zara, counted 13,363 Catholics and 15,000 non-Catholics, with 19 parishes and bishops recorded back to 877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-de-alma:
Diego de Almagro the Elder was, by common report, a foundling. He reached Panama in 1514 and joined Pizarro in the venture that would conquer Peru. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry recounts the partnership of 1524, sealed by a written pact two years later. Both men signed with their marks, since neither could write his name.

Almagro lost an eye to an arrow in a coastal landing. He sailed south for first news of Peru and twice turned back to Panama for stores and men. In doing so he saved Pizarro and his followers from ruin. The entry carries the story through the conquest and the bitter quarrels that followed, pointing readers to the chronicles of Almagro and his son.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elena-lucrezi:
Elena Lucrezia Piscopia Cornaro was a learned Venetian noblewoman, born in 1646 and dead at Padua in 1684. Daughter of Giovanni Battista Cornaro, Procurator of Saint Mark's, she began Latin and Greek at seven and soon mastered them. She went on to Hebrew, Spanish, French, and Arabic, earning the title Oracle of Seven Tongues, and she also studied mathematics, philosophy, and theology.

In 1665 she took the habit of a Benedictine oblate without becoming a nun. At her father's wish she entered Padua University and took a doctorate in philosophy in the cathedral on 25 June 1678, before a crowd of scholars and nobles. A member of several academies and honoured across Europe, she spent her last seven years in study and charity. Her writings, printed at Parma in 1688, mix discourses, translations, and devotional pieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernan-caball:
Fernan Caballero was the pen name of the Spanish novelist Cecilia Bohl von Faber. Born in Switzerland in 1796, she reached Spain with her parents in 1813. Thrice married and widowed, she retired to Seville's royal palace after 1863. Her first novel, La Gaviota, appeared in serial form in 1849.

La Gaviota, The Sea Gull in English, won readers across Europe and beyond. Her novels pictured Andalusian types and customs with charm, grace, and exactness. Critics compared her descriptive power to those of Scott and Cooper. Her complete works filled thirteen volumes published at Madrid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-lop:
Francisco Lopez-Caro, born at Seville in 1598 and dead at Madrid in 1662, was a Spanish portrait painter about whom very little is known. He studied under Juan de las Roelas, painter of the great altarpiece at St. Isidore in Seville and the Martyrdom of St. Andrew in the Seville museum, and practised painting at Seville with indifferent success until about 1660, when he moved to Madrid for his remaining years.

His son and pupil Francisco Caro, born at Seville in 1627 and dead at Madrid in 1667, entered Alonso Cano's studio and considerably surpassed his father. His most important works show scenes from the life of Our Lady in the chapel of St. Isidore in St. Andrew's church, Madrid, and his largest painting, on the Portiuncula indulgence and jubilee for the Franciscan convent at Segovia, includes portraits of its donors, Senor and Senora de Contreras.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-piz:
Francisco Pizarro, born at Trujillo in Estremadura probably in 1471 and dead at Lima on 26 June 1541, was the illiterate conqueror of Peru. Illegitimate son of Gonzalo Pizarro, an infantry captain of the Neapolitan wars, and Francisca Gonzalez, who neglected his schooling, he grew up unable to read or write. Drawn by tales of Spanish exploits in America, he sailed in 1509 with Ojeda to Uraba and held San Sebastian for him. He joined Enciso at Cartagena and crossed Panama with Balboa to first sight the Pacific in 1513.

After Balboa's execution he served Pedrarias Davila, subdued tribes in Veraguas, and in 1522 heard accounts of a rich southern empire. With Diego de Almagro and the priest Hernando de Luque he planned the conquest of Peru and endured years of hardship. In 1532 he seized the Inca Atahuallpa at Cajamarca, holding him for ransom and then executing him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-sav:
Francisco Saverio Clavigero, born at Vera Cruz in Mexico on 9 September 1731 and dead at Bologna on 2 April 1787, was a Jesuit historian of ancient Mexico. Entering the Society at seventeen, he was directed by Father Campoi at the College of St. Peter and St. Paul in Mexico to the documents on Mexican history and antiquities collected by Siguenza y Gongora. He became an enthusiastic investigator. Expelled with the Jesuits from Mexico in 1767, he settled at Bologna, founded a literary academy, and pursued his documentary studies.

There he compiled his Ancient History of Mexico, published at Cesena in 1780, written against De Pauw, Raynal, and Robertson, who had belittled American peoples. Following Boturini, he listed sources with care for Indian pictographs on tissue and other materials and for Indian writers. His systematic arrangement, clear style, and sympathy for the conquered peoples won his book lasting favour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galtelli-nuor:
Galtelli-Nuoro, a diocese in Sardinia's Sassari province, joins an old hill see with a highland town. Galtelli became a bishopric in 1138 under Innocent II, was suppressed by Alexander VI in 1495 and folded into Cagliari, then restored in 1787, though its bishop still lives at Nuoro. The diocese counts twenty-five parishes and 56,300 Catholics.

Nuoro, the ancient Nora, stands some 2,000 feet above the sea amid granite and lead quarries. Near it rise twenty-four Nuraghi, huge truncated cones of the Stone Age known as Giants' Tombs, wonders even to the ancients. Close by lie the Domos de Janas, rooms cut from living granite and linked together. Red jasper quarries and an old cathedral with fine paintings complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guigues-du-ch:
Guigues du Chastel, born in Dauphiné in 1083 or 1084, became fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse in 1110 and gave the young Carthusian order its laws. When he took office only two charterhouses existed; nine more rose during his twenty-seven years. That growth forced him to write down the mother-house customs in his Consuetudines of 1127 or 1128.

After an avalanche wrecked the Grande Chartreuse in 1132 he rebuilt it on its present site. A learned organizer praised by St. Bernard and Peter the Venerable, he also wrote a life of St. Hugh of Grenoble, meditations, and letters, edited St. Jerome's letters in a lost edition, and is sometimes called Venerable, though the Bollandists found no trace of a formal cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isernia-and-v:
Isernia, joined with Venafro as one diocese, sits in Molise between Monte Matese and Monte Azzo, on high ground near the Volturno in fertile country. In the Middle Ages it was famed for parchment making, a trade still carried on there. Ancient Aesernia ranked among the chief Samnite cities, fell to Rome in 295 before Christ. Stayed loyal through the Punic and Social wars until forced to yield in 90 before Christ after long resistance.

As the town decayed, Augustus and Nero planted colonies there. Roman remains survive: a bridge, aqueduct traces, and above all the lower courses of high walls in massive polygonal blocks, pre-Roman work. After Lombard invasion it became a countship under Benevento's duke. The entry gives a small Italian see the full weight of Samnite, Roman, and medieval layers beneath it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacopo-sannaz:
Italian and Latin poet Jacopo Sannazaro was born at Naples on 28 July 1458. He died at Rome in August 1530. His family was of Spanish origin and served Charles III of Durazzo. It held the fief of Rocca di Mondragone from the late fourteenth century. He took his name from St Nazarius, on whose feast he was born.

After losing his father young, he lived with his mother at Nocera dei Pagani. Returning to Naples, he studied with Pontanus and joined his academy. There he gained the name Sincerus, often used in letters of the time. He allied closely with Naples' Aragon princes. He followed Federico into exile after Louis XII of France drove him out in 1521. Federico settled at Tours on the French king's generosity. Sannazaro shared that exile and its literary world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaro:
Jaro is a diocese in the Philippine Islands, formerly part of Cebú diocese. It became a separate diocese on 27 May 1865. It comprises Panay and Negros islands, the Romblon, Palawan, and Jolo groups, and on Mindanao the provinces of Zamboanga, Cotabato, and Davao. Its Catholic population exceeds one million. Here and there are some Aglipayan schismatics, and in Mindanao and Jolo many Muslims and some pagans.

In 1909 the diocese counted forty-five native priests, about forty Augustinian and Recollect friars, twenty Mill Hill missioners, and about ten Jesuits. In Jaro city a Lazarist-run diocesan seminary trains eighty students for priesthood, with the rest preparing for secular careers. At Iloilo city Augustinians run a college for lay students. Academies for young women stand at Jaro, Iloilo, Zamboanga, and Dumaguete. The entry presents a vast island diocese at work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-bicla:
John of Biclaro was a Visigothic chronicler whose history is the fullest and most reliable authority on King Leovigild's reign. Born in Portugal about the middle of the sixth century, he studied Latin and Greek at Constantinople for at least seven years. Returning home, he refused to join the Arian state church and was banished by Leovigild to Barcelona.

After Leovigild died in 586, John founded Biclaro's Benedictine monastery. He ruled it as abbot until he became Bishop of Gerona, attending synods at Saragossa in 592, Barcelona in 599, and Egara in 614. His chronicle, continuing Victor of Tunnuna from 567 to 590, tells the stormy story of the Visigothic conversion from Arianism to Catholicism with religious impartiality despite his own sufferings. Mommsen's 1893 edition remains the best.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-romero:
Juan Romero was a Spanish Jesuit missionary and authority on Guaraní. Born at Machena in Andalusia in 1559, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1580, reached Peru in January 1590, and served as superior of the Tucumán missions from 1593 to 1598. After serving as procurator in Rome, he returned in 1610.

Romero led the Jesuit colleges of Buenos Aires and Santiago del Estero and became first vice-provincial of Chile. In nearly forty years of mission work he gained fluent knowledge of several Indian tongues, above all Guaraní of Paraguay. He also left many letters, shorter papers, and a manuscript treatise on predestination. He died at Santiago, Chile, in 1630.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-herva:
Lorenzo Hervas y Panduro was a Spanish Jesuit and famed student of languages, born at Horcajo in 1735 and dead at Rome in 1809. He taught in Madrid and Murcia, served as a missionary in America until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, and then settled in Italy.

At Cesena and Rome he met Jesuits driven from every corner of the world. He mined their knowledge of remote tongues no books could teach. His huge Idea dell' Universo ran to twenty-one volumes. Its Catalogue of Languages, issued 1800 to 1805, traced peoples by speech: American tongues first, then Pacific island tongues, then Europe's, which he judged weaker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-cancer-d:
Luis Cancer de Barbastro was a Dominican missionary, born in Aragon at an unknown date and killed at Tampa Bay about 1549. One of the first Dominicans to follow Las Casas to Guatemala, he laboured among Vera Paz Indians with zeal and courage.

He wrote songs in Zapotec on the mysteries of faith for Vera Paz converts, a manuscript now lost to view. A staunch ally of Las Casas, he backed him at the Mexico gathering of 1546, then won from Spain charge of converting Florida Indians by peaceful means. Sailing from Vera Cruz in 1549 with two fellow Dominicans, he was betrayed by their interpreter Magdalen, and all three priests were slain on reaching shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mayotte-nossi:
The prefecture apostolic of Mayotte, Nossi-Be, and Comoro covers the Comoro archipelago, the Satellites of Madagascar. Mayotte, the farthest south and most important of the Comoros, stands with Anjuan, Mohilla, and Great Comoro, plus Nossi-Be and Santa Maria. The islands look like cones of drowned groves, cut from the mainland by deep gulfs.

Heights run from Mayotte's 1,800 feet to Anjuan's 5,000 and Great Comoro's volcanic cone above 7,000. Two monsoons bring two seasons, sometimes with cyclones, and the rich soil yields vanilla, cloves, sugar cane, and coffee in plenty. Some 80,000 people live there, mostly Africans, with Sakalavas from Madagascar. The group was for centuries an Arab colony, once very prosperous, and the entry maps its lands, peoples, and church charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-carn:
Melchior Carneiro, a missionary bishop born of a noble Coimbra family, died at Macao in 1583. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1543, became first rector of Evora College in 1551, and soon after took the Lisbon rectorship. When Simon Rodriguez, Portugal's first provincial, was called to Rome to answer charges, the visitor Nadal gave him Carneiro as companion.

King John of Portugal had asked Pope Julius III and St. Ignatius for a Jesuit Patriarch of Ethiopia. The pope chose John Nunez, with Andrew Oviedo and Carneiro as coadjutors with right of succession. Consecrated in 1555, they were the first Jesuits raised to the episcopate. Ignatius accepted, judging the rank a burden of hardship rather than honour. Barred from Ethiopia, Carneiro laboured at Goa and on the Malabar coast until 1567, when he became first bishop of Japan and China, an office he soon gave up.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montefeltro:
Montefeltro, in the province of Urbino in the Marches, first appears as Mona Feretri in the diplomas by which Charlemagne confirmed Pepin's grants to the Holy See. Its counts became imperial vicars in 1135 and Counts of Urbino in 1213, though their rule was broken between 1322 and 1375, and Cardinal Albornoz expelled them again in 1359.

The elder Guido of Montefeltro, a famed Ghibelline captain, ended his life as a Franciscan in 1298. Its first known bishop, Agatho, sat at San Leo in 826, and later bishops built the cathedral, the episcopal palace at Calamello and the seminary at Pennabilli, where the see eventually settled. The diocese, suffragan of Urbino, follows its bishops and shifting seats through the centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montenegro:
Montenegro is a kingdom on the Adriatic's east coast in the Balkans, once part of Roman Dalmatia. Diocletian carved out the province of Praevalis there, with Dioclea as capital. From the seventh century Serb tribes settled the land, founding principalities called zupanates. The southernmost was Zeta, later Duklja, cradle of the Nemanjic family.

Stefan I Nemanja, recognised as chief zupan in 1165, embraced Orthodoxy and organised the Serbian Church. His son Sava, first Orthodox Archbishop of Serbia in 1221, founded a see for Zeta near Cattaro. Under Stefan Dusan the Balsic family governed Zeta, then the Crnojevic line resisted them. After the Serbian Empire fell, the mountain land kept its independence against Turks and Venetians, with its prince-bishops and later kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nero:
Nero, the last Julian-Claudian emperor, reigned from 54 to 68 as son of Domitius Ahenobarbus and Julia Agrippina, niece of Claudius. After Messalina's violent death, Claudius married Julia, adopted her son Nero, and gave him his daughter Octavia in marriage. Agrippina, ready for any crime to enthrone her son, had Seneca made his tutor and Burrus commander of the Praetorian guard.

Born at Antium on 15 December 37, Nero was seventeen at his accession, believing himself a great singer and poet, his better nature stifled by sensuality and moral perversity. Agrippina hoped to share his rule, but her autocratic temper soon ended that. His first years, directed by Burrus and Seneca, the real holders of power, were auspicious, easing taxation and provincial abuses. The entry follows his later crimes, the fire of Rome, persecution of Christians, and his fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicastro:
Nicastro is a city of Catanzaro province in Calabria, southern Italy, on a promontory commanding the Gulf of Saint Euphemia, with an ancient castle above. Its port exports acid, herbs and wine. The cathedral, an ancient temple, with the episcopal palace, stood outside the city. Saracens pillaged it, it was restored in 1100, then destroyed in the 1638 earthquake with the palace, losing most valuable archives under the ruins.

The Greek Rite long prevailed at Nicastro. Its first recorded bishop was Henry in 1090. Tancredo da Monte Foscolo, deposed by Honorius IV for crowning John of Aragon King of Sicily, was reinstated by Boniface VIII. Paolo Capisucco judged Henry VIII's marriage case, Marcello Cervino became Pope Marcellus II, and Giovanni Tommaso Perrone built the new cathedral. In 1818 Martorano joined the diocese, suffragan of Reggio, with 52 parishes and 110,100 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pesaro:
Pesaro was an Adriatic city at the Foglia's mouth, living by fishing, farming, majolica, and mining. Its cathedral of San Francesco carries a Gothic portal and Bellini's Coronation of the Madonna, while San Domenico holds the tomb of the poet Giulio Perticari. The Ducal Palace, begun by Laurana before 1465, and the Almerici museum of inscriptions, coins, ivories, and majolica anchor its civic pride.

Senones held the town until Rome drove them out in 283 BC, and it became a colony in 184. Gothic War sieges battered it, Lombards took it four times, and it passed to the Papal States. Malatesta lords gave way to the Sforza, when Galeazzo Malatesta settled Pesaro as dower on his niece Costanza Varano. Rossini, born here, is honoured by its music school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piero-da-san-:
Piero della Francesca was the great realist painter of the early Renaissance, born at Borgo San Sepolcro about 1420. Son of the notary Ser Benedetto, he worked at Perugia in 1438, probably under Domenico Veneziano, and at Sant'Egidio in Florence in 1439 and 1440. Domenico and Paolo Uccello shaped his art. He emerged as an independent master in 1445 with a many-panelled altarpiece for his town's Misericordia brotherhood.

At Rimini in 1451 he painted Sigismondo Malatesta venerating his patron, and between about 1460 and 1466 he created his masterpiece, the Arezzo choir frescoes of the True Cross. His Resurrection at Borgo, his Baptism and moonlit Nativity in London, and his perspective treatise, Prospettiva Pingendi, made him the age's master of perspective and light. Perugino's generation learned from him. He died at home in 1492.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-policastro:
Policastro is a diocese in the province of Salerno in southern Italy, on a hill above the gulf that bears its name. It is the ancient Pituntia and continues the Diocese of Buxentum, whose first known bishop was Rusticus in 501. It is suffragan to Salerno and counts thirty-eight parishes with 64,000 people.

Its bishops include Gabriele Atilio, a Latin poet of 1471, and Urbano Felicio, who held a synod in 1630. Vincenzo de Sylva, besieged in his palace by Count Carafa for defending church rights, remodelled the see, while Tommaso and Antonio della Rosa restored cathedral and seminary. The present bishop at the entry's writing was Mgr. Vescia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-queretaro:
Queretaro, a diocese in Mexico under Michoacan, covers the state of the same name: 4,492 square miles, with 243,515 people by the census of 1910. This encyclopedia entry names its chief city, home of bishop and governor, as Querétaro itself, with 35,011 people in 1910. Otomi Indians founded the city in 1446, and Spaniards have held it since 1531. Religious orders arrived in turn: Carmelites in 1601, Dieguinos in 1613, Fathers of Mercy in 1636, and Dominicans in 1692.

Augustinians and Fathers of the Oratory of Saint Philip also kept houses there. The Jesuit college of Saint Francis Xavier fell in 1767, when Charles the Third expelled all Jesuits from Spanish lands. One institution outshone the rest: the college of Apostolic missionaries, which Innocent the Eleventh called the greatest influence for spreading the faith, sending missioners far beyond Mexico, even to Upper California. Vera, Noriega and Domenech supply the entry's Mexican sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raimundo-dios:
Raimundo Diosdado Caballero, miscellaneous writer chiefly on church topics, was born at Palma in Majorca on 19 June 1740. This encyclopedia entry gives his death at Rome uncertainly, as either 16 January 1830 or 28 April 1829. He entered the Society of Jesus on 15 November 1752. He held the literature chair at the Jesuit College in Madrid for several years. He was deported to Italy with the other Jesuits when the Society was suppressed in Spanish lands.

In his new home Father Caballero pursued a varied literary career. His chief works include a study of the first age of Spanish printing, printed at Rome in 1793, and critical notes of 1798 that correct Schelstrate and Hardouin. In the latter he argues that the native tongue of Christ and the Apostles was Syriac, not Greek, against Dominicus Diodati. Later writings treat Mexican history, closer union between American and European Spaniards, and American considerations, with Sommervogel and Hurter as sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rio-negro:
Rio Negro was a prefecture apostolic in Brazil, carved from the See of Amazones by a decree of October 1910. It was bounded on the south by the watershed between the Rio Negro and the Rio Branco. On other sides lay Colombia and Venezuela and the territory of Rio Branco. The white population was small, confined to a few villages along the Rio Negro itself.

Mission history reaches back to 1658, when the Jesuit Francisco Gonsales founded a mission for the peoples of the Upper Rio Negro. Traces of Jesuit work still survived in scattered villages. A Carmelite evangelized the Tucumaos two years later. From 1870 the Franciscans laboured among the Indians, with seven stations on the Uaupes, four on the Tikie, and one on the Papuri. When the empire fell, most missions were abandoned, though some were later restored.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-severo:
San Severo, a diocese in Foggia province in southern Italy, lies on a fertile plain watered by the Radicosa and Triolo rivers. Its city's origin is obscure. Under the Normans it housed a prince, then passed to the Benedictines of Torre Maggiore and later to the Templars, whose suppression broke up its lands. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a see through earthquakes and transfers.

Quakes struck hard in 1627, 1828, and 1851. The diocese, set up in 1580, merely continues Civitate, which itself succeeded ancient Teanum. At Civitate papal troops lost to the Normans in 1052, and its bishops included the theologian Lorenzo da Viterbo, the astronomer Luca Gaurico, and Francesco Alciato, later cardinal. Martino de Martini, a Jesuit, became San Severo's first bishop in 1580.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santiago-del-:
Santiago del Estero, an Argentine diocese erected on 25 March 1907 as suffragan of Buenos Aires, exactly matches its home state. It is bounded by Salta, Tucumán, La Rioja, Córdoba, Santa Fe, and the Chaco territory. It covers nearly 40,000 square miles with about five people per square mile. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia notes a paradox: the newest diocese holds the oldest see.

Santiago city, on the Dulce river forty miles north of the Great Salt Marshes, hosted the first bishop in that part of South America. Church organisation in the future Argentina began in 1570 under Pius V, who erected the diocese of Tucumán over a vast, barely explored land. The entry follows that original diocese's slow division into the modern sees of the north-west.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sao-sebastiao:

euthyphro:
Plato's Euthyphro, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, meets Socrates outside the king archon's court, where he awaits trial for impiety. my-friend-prospero:

nasa-tm-19660009052-nasa-s-spacecraft-ba:

nasa-tm-19660015353-rocket-measurements-:

Ground cameras see the glow, but not the particles causing it. Rocket data link the two views together. Evans presents measurements from the zone where displays are brightest. Such flights built the base of facts about how energy from the magnetosphere reaches the air above the poles.

nasa-tm-19660024052-experimental-perform:

nasa-tm-19700025079-a-design-parameter-s:

nasa-tm-19710000918-scattering-of-42-mev:

nasa-tm-19710007274-topics-in-solar-cosm:

nasa-tm-19710018370-a-concept-for-a-lear:

no-hero:

A day and night in Syria leads to Jaffa and Jerusalem. Alexandria and Cairo close the road. Thackeray narrates with ease and irony.

the-life-studies-and-works-of-benjamin-w:
John Galt composed the life, studies, and works of Benjamin West from materials West furnished himself, in a book dated 1820. His preface, dated April 25, 1816, explains a change of plan. West later career belongs so fully to the public history of art that Galt detached the early memoirs as a whole by themselves.

West rose without a teacher, and Galt argues that his self taught path helps young artists more than fine lectures could. West served as president of the Royal Academy in London. Part one follows an American painter from colonial beginnings toward history painting fame.
the-little-colonel-s-hero: The Little Colonel's Hero by Annie Fellows Johnston carries a 1902 copyright from the Page Company of Boston, with a frontispiece by Etheldred B. Barry. The dedication addresses all the friends of the Little Colonel whose letters the author could not answer. Printed impression lists run from the twenty-seventh in 1925 to the thirty-fifth in 1937, showing how long the book stayed in print.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Volume six of Suetonius's Lives of the Twelve Caesars covers Nero Claudius Caesar, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester. Suetonius opens with the Domitii, the family behind Nero. One branch, the Aenobarbi, took both descent and name from Lucius Domitius, whose black hair was stroked by two godlike young men announcing a victory, and turned the bright color of brass.

That mark, Suetonius says, descended to his posterity, who generally had red beards. The family collected seven consulships, one triumph, and two censorships. They also used only two first names, Cneius and Lucius, swapping them in an irregular pattern across generations. Family pride and oddity come first, before Nero's own story begins.
the-negro:

the-water-supply-of-the-el-paso-and-sout:
J. L. Campbell presented his paper on the El Paso and Southwestern Railway's water supply to the American Society of Civil Engineers in May 1910. The described system serves the division between Carrizozo and Santa Rosa in New Mexico, a distance of 128 miles across arid country west of the hundredth meridian. Discussion by G. E. P. Smith and Kenneth Allan accompanies the paper.

Average annual precipitation is given as 9.84 inches, and exceptionally dry 1909 saw less than five. Wells from 100 to 1,100 feet deep originally supplied the road, but their water stayed bad after thorough treatment. Campbell lists the damage plainly: violent foaming, hard scaling, destroyed boiler tubes, engine failures, and demoralised train service.
young-folks-treasury-volume-2-of-12-myth: Hamilton Wright Mabie edited this twelve-volume Young Folks' Treasury, with Edward Everett Hale as associate editor.
